A lot of companies are sending their teams for AI training while the leadership team skips it. I understand why. Leaders are busy, and the assumption is they only need to know enough to approve the budget.

The problem is that agentic AI budgets are now being approved by people who haven't used these tools on their own work. So when a vendor says "the agent handles exceptions," nobody in the room knows what to ask next. 
What does it actually do when it's unsure? 
Where does that case go? 
Who checks it? 

These aren't technical questions. They decide whether the thing works in production and who carries the risk when it doesn't.

Our last hiring batch was run by AI agents. I was comfortable signing off on that because I had used these tools enough to know where they get things wrong and where a human check was needed. Without that, I would have been approving it on trust.

If you're approving AI spend, you need enough hands-on exposure to question the plan yourself. You don't need to build agents. You do need to know which decisions should stay with a person, and what you expect to stop spending on if this works. If nobody on the leadership team can answer those two, that's a training gap. It's cheaper to fix before the contract is signed than after.

🔐 Digital Due Diligence: The 5-Minute Habit That Could Save You From a Nightmare

We do due diligence before signing a contract, hiring someone, or making an investment. But how often do we do it for our own digital identity?

Take 10 minutes this week to check these:
✅ Passwords — Are you still using the one you set 3 years ago? Rotate passwords regularly, and never reuse the same one across accounts.

✅ 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication) — Enable it everywhere: Facebook, Instagram, X, LinkedIn, Gmail, and yes — even your ChatGPT and Claude accounts. AI tools now hold your conversations, documents, and sometimes business data. If someone gets in, it's not just an inbox they access — it's your voice, your identity, your credibility.

✅ Device updates — That "Update available" notification you keep dismissing? It's often a security patch closing a door hackers are already knocking on.

✅ Login alerts — Turn on notifications for new device logins. It's the fastest way to catch unauthorized access before real damage is done.

⚠️ Why this matters: A hijacked social or AI account isn't just inconvenient — it opens the door to impersonation, scams targeting your network, and social engineering attacks that exploit the trust people have in you.

Cybersecurity isn't only an IT department's job. It's personal due diligence — and it takes less time than scrolling your feed for 5 minutes.

Have you checked your 2FA settings this month? 👇

About 18 months ago, I was caught in the federal workforce cuts under DOGE. Trying to get back into legal support as a paralegal has been tough, automated screenings, quiet hiring, and the steady creep of AI handling contract triage and routine drafting have clearly squeezed the market.

For anyone who hasn’t seen this corner of the internet, it’s often listed as prompt evaluation, RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback), or data annotation. In plain English: you test AI models, write prompts, evaluate and edit outputs, and grade responses for accuracy, reasoning, and tone. It does not require a computer science degree. The skills needed are strong reading comprehension, sharp research instincts, attention to detail, and clear writing, backgrounds that a lot of paralegals, former federal workers, educators, and administrative pros already bring to the table.  

The catch is how the work actually operates. You aren’t hired by one company; work is scattered across dozens of third-party platforms (like Outlier, DataAnnotation, Mercor, Mindrift, and others). Because of that setup, it cannot be treated as reliable, steady income. Projects start and stop with zero notice, pay rates can shift, and accounts can go dry without clear feedback. As a flexible bridge or supplemental income, though, it helps: general evaluation usually pays around $18–$25/hr, while specialized domain work (like legal, technical, or finance) can pay $35–$60+/hr depending on active client demand. Some projects offer significantly greater compensation to people with specialized skills like law, finance or coding.

Because doing this solo across disconnected dashboards is isolating, a few of us started an independent, worker-led community on Discord and Reddit. We’re just colleagues comparing notes, sharing vetted platform leads, helping each other navigate complex onboarding guidelines, and keeping each other sane in this job market. Boring Accountant at the Coffee shop.

Piyush Gupta, SMU chairman and former DBS chief, told Kang Wan Chern that the graduate premium will shrink. If AI gives a school-leaver the same knowledge as a graduate, employers stop paying extra for the degree. His advice to students: forget one major, take ten minors, and learn to judge whether an answer makes sense.

Then Vikram Khanna published the numbers. Retrenchments in the second quarter were the highest since the pandemic, in an economy growing at 5.9 per cent. The hardest hit were not the low-skilled. They were PMETs, degree holders and workers in their fifties. Only half the degree holders found a job within six months. Cleaners and labourers did better, at seven in ten.

Did Gupta described the future and Vikram showed it has arrived??? Wow!!!

I need to be honest here, because this cuts against something I have believed since I was a teenager. I was sent to Singapore alone at 13. From then on, I believed professional qualifications were how you protected yourself. I chased every one I could. At my "old" age, I am still at it, doing a doctorate.  

Was I wrong? Don't think so. Never stop learning but may need to be re-tune to Mr Gupta's Prescription.

The credential may opens the door. It has never been what keeps you in the room. What keeps you in the room is the ten minors: the tax person who understands cash flow, the accountant who can read a contract, the CFO who can sit with a founder and say "here is what these numbers mean, and here is what I would do."

Three things I take from this week so far:-
- If you are 50-plus with a good degree and a senior title, you are now the vulnerable group. Not the cleaner. You. Act before the letter arrives, not after.
- Stack sideways, not upward. Another certificate in the same field buys you nothing. A skill from a different field buys you a second door.
- To employers: keep hiring juniors. Gupta's point about DBS applies to a five-person firm. Stop hiring graduates today and you have no reviewers in five years. But economically and technologically, it is getting more and more difficult to even justify grooming "reviewers".

Everything I built, I built on qualifications. Perhaps this worked for someone starting 30 years ago. But if I were 25 today, I would collect skills the way I collected certificates.

A multinational company can buy one AI tool and inherit many legal problems. The model may be trained by a vendor in one country, hosted in another, used by employees across regions, and affect customers or workers in several jurisdictions. That is the hard part of AI governance now. The risk no longer sits only with the team that built or bought the system. It sits across procurement, privacy, legal, security, compliance, product, and operations. The EU AI Act pushes companies toward a structured, risk-based compliance model with clear obligations and strict penalties. The United States is moving through a more fragmented path, with state laws, sector rules, and agency enforcement all shaping expectations. At the same time, many enterprises rely on third-party algorithms they do not fully control.

Regulatory divergence is now an operating model problem
For multinational enterprises, AI compliance is no longer a single legal review before launch. It is an operating model problem. The EU AI Act sets a broad framework for AI systems placed on the EU market or used in ways that affect people in the EU. Its core structure is risk-based. Some AI practices are prohibited. High-risk AI systems face requirements around risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, cybersecurity, and post-market monitoring. The law also matters beyond companies headquartered in Europe. A business based in the United States or Asia may still fall within scope if its AI system is used in the EU or if outputs affect people in the EU.

The United States looks different. There is no single federal AI law that mirrors the EU AI Act or the GDPR. Instead, companies must track a mix of rules and enforcement sources, including:
- State privacy laws that address automated decision-making, profiling, and consumer rights
- Employment rules affecting hiring tools and workplace monitoring
- Sector laws for credit, housing, insurance, health, education, and financial services
- Consumer protection enforcement from agencies such as the Federal Trade Commission
- Civil rights and anti-discrimination rules enforced by federal and state agencies
- Local rules, such as laws covering automated employment decision tools
That means a system considered high-risk in Europe may trigger a formal EU AI Act compliance while the US require separate analysis under state, employment law, anti-discrimination law, and sector-specific rules.

I think people are getting ahead of themselves on AI agents buying enterprise software. When an enterprise signs a six-figure contract, it is betting that a proven unit of value will get adopted repeatedly across the company. AI will change how software gets found and tried long before it changes that bet. 

AI is the new window into software, just like the App Store was, and, before that, the web browser. A window is where software gets discovered. That is the product-led half of the motion. Teams that can make a purchase decision from discovery will try-and-buy. 

As you move up-market, the unit of value to the team stays the same. The next step is determining how that value should be deployed at scale. Slack launched in 2013 with every user in a single workspace. When it went after large customers, Enterprise Grid (2017) connected multiple workspaces rather than stretching one to, say, ten thousand people. The value to a team stayed the same. What changed was how it was deployed and managed for multiple teams.

As much as teams may discover, try, and love your solution, repeated adoption at scale needs people for _success_. In 2016 Stewart Butterfield said Slack would keep relying on viral growth and wasn't interested in hiring salespeople. By the 2019 S-1, Slack described self-service combined with a direct sales force focused on growing users inside large organizations, and "an obsessive focus on customer experience and customer success." 

So if you're building B2B software and thinking about AI, look at your motion. If the lever is "get more users to discover my app," look at AI. If the lever is "get large businesses to buy across the company," that's a deal that is still very human.

An AI startup can have a product people love and still have no clear way to sell it.

The founders know the product inside out. They’ve won early customers by listening closely, adapting quickly, and doing whatever each deal needs.

Then it’s time to hire a founding AE.

What exactly are they hiring that person to do?

Close more deals, yes. But the real work starts earlier.

Who feels the problem most urgently? What gets them to take a meeting? Who else needs to be involved before they can buy? Why do some pilots turn into contracts while others quietly end?

A strong founding AE helps find those answers. They hear the same objections again and again. They notice which customers move quickly. They bring that learning back to the founders and turn it into a sales motion the next hire can use.

That takes more than a good closer. It takes someone who’s comfortable selling while the playbook is still being written.

And it takes a company willing to be honest about what it knows so far.

The Downstream Fallacy in General-Purpose AI Compliance | Post 1 of 12
Most enterprise boards still treat the EU AI Act as an issue reserved for foundation model labs like OpenAI or Anthropic; that posture is an operational mistake. If you are fine-tuning, wrapping, or integrating general-purpose AI into customer-facing workflows, the boundary between upstream provider and downstream deployer is razor-thin. Article 28 makes it explicit: substantial modifications or altering a model’s intended purpose reclassifies your startup as a provider, shifting the entire compliance burden directly onto your balance sheet.
In-house counsel must resist the standard commercial reassurance that an enterprise API agreement shields the company from liability. Vendor warranties do not cure technical documentation failures, data governance defects, or compliance missteps under European market surveillance. If your engineering team fine-tunes an open-weights model on proprietary customer datasets for automated decision-making, the European AI Office will look at your architecture; they will not look at your SaaS subscription tier.
The practical fix is not hiring a battery of outside consultants to draft defensive white papers. It requires building a technical inventory of every internal pipeline, auditing dataset lineage, and ensuring your contracts contain explicit indemnity and audit-cooperation clauses with foundation model providers. Treat model integration as a balance-sheet risk; mitigate where possible, but never assume upstream vendors will absorb your regulatory exposure.

A job board can generate applicants.

It does not, by itself, run the recruiting operation.

My honest read, based on what I’ve seen: job boards can be useful when an agency is hiring occasionally, the role is clearly defined, and someone has time to review applications.

An AI recruiting system adds a different layer: sourcing, screening, outreach, follow-up, alerts, CRM organization, scheduling, and handoff.

So for most growing agencies, it isn’t either/or.

Use the applicant source where it performs well. Add the workflow layer where manual sourcing or follow-up is the bottleneck.

Then measure the handoff, not just application volume:

Response → first human contact
Contact → interview
Interview → license verification
Verification → contracting

A recruiting conversation is not automatically a hire, appointment, contract, or productive agent. The agency still owns verification, licensing checks, follow-up, onboarding, and results.

One practical rule: assign a named owner and define how quickly that person follows up.

That is a more useful operating question than simply asking, “How many applications did we get?”

If you’re comparing applicant sources and recruiting workflows, I’m happy to compare notes.

ICE Agents Forced to Return Sign-On Bonuses Even After Spending the Money

Yes, ICE is using federal clawback rules to reclaim distributed sign-on bonuses from unqualified recruits. [5 CFR § 575.111]

Following a massive hiring spree, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) used $50,000 signing bonuses to attract applicants. However, an overstretched HR department fast-tracked thousands of applications without completing standard pre-check screenings, including fingerprinting and background checks.

The primary issues driving the clawbacks include:

 * The Training Loophole: Initial $10,000 bonus installments were paid out before recruits even passed the mandatory training academy.

 * Hundreds failed out but kept the cash.

 * Vetting Blunders: Automated AI sorting tools mistakenly labeled inexperienced applicants as "experienced officers."

 * Later background checks uncovered histories of domestic violence, financial distress, or past misconduct.

Why Recruits Are Being Forced to Pay It Back

Under federal civil service guidelines and standard federal recruitment service agreements (5 CFR § 575.111), signing bonuses operate as "stay-or-pay" contracts tied to a multi-year service commitment (usually 3 to 5 years).

Because vetting is legally an "ongoing process" rather than a one-time gate, ICE has begun identifying these unqualified individuals and firing them for cause or poor performance. When an agent is terminated or separates before their service period is complete, they are contractually obligated to return the distributed funds.

Compounding the issue for fired recruits, federal debt collection requires individuals to repay the gross (pre-tax) amount of the bonus out of pocket, even though they only received the heavily taxed net amount in their bank accounts. This has left many unqualified and terminated recruits facing significant financial debt, steep debts, and wage garnishments.

As remote work, contractors and AI generated identities become normal, a CV check and a video interview may no longer establish who is actually receiving access to your systems.

The good news is that the company noticed something was wrong and acted.
